historical_timeline.summary: Born Joseph Louis Barrow near LaFayette, Alabama.
Family moves to Detroit; he later takes up boxing.
Wins the heavyweight championship; holds it until he retires as champion in 1949.
Enlists in the U.S. Army; serves through the war, boxing exhibitions for the troops.
Owes more than $1 million in federal back taxes, penalties and interest.
Collapses on a Manhattan street; later attributes it to cocaine; troubled by fears of a plot against his life.
Hospitalized for about five months in Denver for paranoid delusions.
Arterial graft surgery for an aortic aneurysm; afterwards uses a wheelchair; later strokes and a pacemaker.
Works as an official greeter at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas.
Dies of cardiac arrest in the Las Vegas area; buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Cocaine use disorder with a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder in a 55-year-old Black man, a retired heavyweight champion and Army veteran, who comes in two weeks after collapsing in the street, with persecutory fears and little sleep. The episode covers a nonjudgmental assessment with DSM-5-TR criteria, the DAST-10 and urine drug testing with consent; the differential between a substance-induced psychosis, a primary psychotic disorder and a neurocognitive disorder after a long boxing career, using the time course after the last use, the MoCA, laboratory tests and brain MRI, and the plain fact that traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis; a structured assessment that guards against the documented bias toward diagnosing schizophrenia in Black men; a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; aripiprazole when psychosis persists, with metabolic and movement monitoring under the APA guideline and a taper after remission; contingency management and cognitive behavioral therapy as the ASAM/AAAP guideline advises, since no medicine is approved by the FDA for cocaine use disorder; fentanyl in the stimulant supply, naloxone and fentanyl test strips; the cardiovascular risks of cocaine with an ECG, creatine kinase, home blood pressure, a diagnosis of hypertension and an echocardiogram that measures the aortic root; a one-day return to use met without blame; involving family only with his consent; and help with financial stress through social work and free taxpayer services.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Louis returns one week after intake and is seen by Dr. Featherstone-Ibe of addiction psychiatry on the same day. assessment.display: Cocaine use disorder, severe, with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder
assessment.assessment: Seven DSM-5-TR criteria make a severe cocaine use disorder. The delusions began during heavy use, he has never had psychotic symptoms without cocaine, they are already fading after ten days, and the examination, laboratory tests and MRI show no other cause: this is a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. A primary psychotic disorder becomes likelier only if symptoms persist beyond about a month without cocaine, and the diagnosis of schizophrenia, which is made too often in Black men, should not be made on a first presentation like this

assessment.display: Cognition after a long boxing career
assessment.assessment: A MoCA of 25 after three hours of sleep and during active psychosis does not show a neurocognitive disorder; the MRI is normal. Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis under the NINDS consensus criteria, not a clinical one, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy can be confirmed only after death, so neither label belongs in his record. The MoCA should be repeated when he has slept well and been well for some weeks

Symptoms that persist after ten days without cocaine and keep him from sleeping justify an antipsychotic, as the ASAM/AAAP guideline advises. Aripiprazole at a low dose has little effect on weight, glucose, prolactin and the QT interval, which suits a man with raised blood pressure and a borderline lipid profile. Watch for akathisia. After a period of remission, a gradual taper is advised for a stimulant-induced psychosis

No medicine is approved by the FDA for cocaine use disorder. Contingency management is the treatment with the strongest evidence and should be the core of his plan, with cognitive behavioral therapy alongside it. The off-label options in the guideline, such as topiramate or bupropion, can wait while he does well, and the stimulant-based ones (modafinil, or topiramate with extended-release amphetamine) are unsafe after a psychosis and with high blood pressure

assessment.display: Raised blood pressure and cardiovascular risk
assessment.assessment: Cocaine raises blood pressure and the risk of heart attack, stroke, arrhythmia and aortic dissection. His blood pressure remains raised ten days after his last use, and the ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage, so hypertension is likely; it should be confirmed with home readings once he has been without cocaine for some weeks. Beta-blockers are best avoided while he may still use cocaine

Fentanyl contaminates much of the illicit stimulant supply, and people who do not use opioids have died of it; naloxone and test strips are essential. He has no suicidal or homicidal ideation and no access to firearms, and he is safe to treat as an outpatient with weekly visits. Family can help, but only with his consent and on his terms
